name: consistency-violation-second-processor
description: A `create` of a second `processor` element. Nothing about the payload is wrong — it is exactly what discovery declares for the kind — and the identity is free, so neither the schema pass nor the identity pass has anything to say. What the assembled staged result breaks is the contract's one-processor rule, `hardware.multiple-processors`, which is a statement about the layer as a whole and therefore only checkable once the whole result exists.

context.summary: The `examples/basic` model, whose `hardware/` layer declares exactly one processor, `CPU`. The change set adds `CPU2` beside it.

authorization.notes: The scope covers the create exactly, so the refusal is the model rule and not the authorization boundary.

expected.notes: BOTH processors are named, and neither is called the offender: the rule is that the layer holds one, and choosing which of the two to delete is a decision the rule does not make and the model cannot make for the architect. That is the same reason `hardware.no-processor` — the other half of the same rule — is reported against the layer itself, which has no element to name at all. A client repairs this by removing either address in a change set of its own.
